source.title: Probability-Signature Dynamics: Unpacking Modular Addition Learning Within Two-Layer Networks
source.authors: Yun-Jing Wang; Jun-Jie Yao; Lin-Yu Liu; Pin-Yan Lu; Zhi-qin John Xu

record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes modular-addition training dynamics using probability signatures and reports experiments on generalization and Fourier-structured neurons. This is a conceptual test of the grokking mechanism, not an explicit replication of the original training recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper reports accuracy outcomes under weight-decay settings, neuron norm and Fourier-sparsity measurements, frequency/phase alignment, and a full-batch frequency comparison. Cited findings from other work are excluded. Supplementary parameter sweeps are not treated as evidence for delayed generalization on non-algorithmic data: the text does not report that behavior there.
record.test_reason: The study measures how Fourier-structured neurons form during modular-addition training. It tracks neuron norm against Fourier sparsity, the clean-versus-noise drive, and the emergence of frequency and phase alignment. This bears on V2's gradual-circuit account. It also varies weight decay, which bears on V5's low-norm bias. It never measures the generalization delay itself, so V1 is effectively untested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that probability signatures, conditional statistics of the training data, are diagonalized by the Fourier basis in modular addition. This yields decoupled mode dynamics that explain dominant frequencies, frequency matching and phase alignment. Label collisions explain the faster early loss decrease on noisy labels, and XOR predicts a Hadamard basis. They also claim weight decay acts as a survival threshold for Fourier structure, which they tie to grokking.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies a two-layer embedding MLP on modular addition, including experiments with corrupted labels and probability-signature gradient analysis. It does not present itself as a replication of the original grokking recipe; its main focus is deriving and testing a forward account of Fourier-mode dynamics.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported training outcomes vary with weight decay; the supplementary accuracy curves also vary initialization scale and optimizer. The paper states that excessive weight decay can prevent convergence and that smaller initialization can shorten training convergence time under appropriate weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Under uniform label noise, noisy examples' loss falls faster early in training than clean examples' loss, at all noise ratios. Bijective noise reverses this when α>0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early memorization speed of corrupted labels is set by conditional label-collision statistics of the training data.

fits_no_version.finding: XOR training produces Hadamard-basis sparse neurons whose growth tracks test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The representation basis learned on group operations is predicted by the common eigenbasis of data probability signatures.

record.problems: The paper says its gradient-flow analysis is an approximation of dominant terms and does not claim validity throughout training. Several accuracy and neuron-structure results are presented in figures without numerical timing or uncertainty estimates. The paper does not vary training-set size, and its main experiments use a single modular-addition setup.
record.rows_left_out: Supplementary optimizer, initialization-scale, activation-function, and XOR plots were not included as separate rows because they do not report the delayed-generalization behavior specified by the tested versions. The paper's cited results from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: The timing of the test jump relative to training saturation is never stated, and training-set size is never varied.
Whether progress measures anticipate a delayed test jump. It is also not shown that the decaying low-sparsity neurons are memorizing components.
Entire version: no non-algorithmic data and no lazy-to-rich test. Initialization scale is varied only in appendix accuracy curves, with no delay measure.
Critical dataset size, ungrokking, and a direct efficiency comparison of the two circuits.
Entire version: Adam and AdamW curves are shown, but optimizer or numerical artifacts are not tested as the cause of a delay.

missing.what: Final accuracy against weight decay across activations: linear barely fits training, tanh generalizes poorly, quadratic and ReLU generalize at suitable λ. This shows weight decay alone does not yield generalization.
Adam and AdamW accuracy and loss curves across λ and γ: no generalization without weight decay, and smaller initialization shortens convergence.
ReLU replication of the neuron norm/sparsity and frequency-phase results.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is about the mechanism of Fourier-mode formation, not about the grokking delay. Its accuracy curves are given without timing numbers, and no delay is quantified anywhere, so V1 cannot be assessed. The training/test split is fixed at 80:20 with label noise, unlike the original recipe. The gradient-approximation cosine similarity (≥0.9) and the 93% truncated-model agreement validate the authors' method and are not results on the claim.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not sweep training-set size or report how delay changes as the set shrinks. The text does not establish the timing of a near-perfect test-accuracy rise after training accuracy saturates.
The paper does not establish that the measured progress quantities anticipate the test-accuracy jump; it reports norm growth and accuracy improvement as simultaneous.
No non-algorithmic dataset or lazy-to-rich transition is tested for grokking-like delays.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning is studied.
The paper does not test a critical dataset-size threshold or ungrokking below it, nor directly compare the efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits.

The frequency comparison uses shared initialization and concerns neurons in a full-batch check; it does not test whether independently trained networks converge to the same algorithm across architectures or hyperparameters.
Adam and AdamW results are shown, but the paper does not test whether adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits produce the delay.

rows.subject: Two-layer embedding MLP (GELU; D = 2000, P = 113)
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition with 10% uniformly random label noise under the stated weight decay.
rows.measure: Accuracy on clean training examples, noisy training examples, and test examples
rows.value: 100% on clean and noise, but 0 on test
rows.note: The caption describes this setting as overfitting. The text does not establish whether a test-accuracy rise occurs later.
rows.check: For V1, no test rise occurs within the 3000-epoch window at λ=0, but V1 says nothing about weight decay, so this is not a timing test. For V5 the row should be marked observed: no low-norm bias means no generalization, as V5 predicts. A single state cannot hold both, so treat the V5 link as observed.

rows.check: Training fails to converge at λ=1e-3, so V1's premise (training accuracy saturates) is unmet and the V1 link should be removed. For V5 it shows that excess weight decay causes failure; this qualifies V5 rather than testing it.

conditions.value: different settings; the text does not assign a specific value to Figure 2

rows.measure: Relationship between neuron norm and Fourier sparsity; growth versus decay by sparsity group
rows.value: The text reports that most neurons' norms continuously decrease to 0, while a few grow; all newly grown neurons have relatively high sparsity, and norm growth is concentrated on high-sparsity neurons.
rows.note: The paper interprets this as weight decay suppressing most neurons while a few high-sparsity neurons grow.

rows.value: The paper says norm growth and accuracy improvement occur simultaneously in time.
rows.note: This reports circuit-associated progress, but does not show that the progress measure anticipates the test-accuracy jump.
rows.check: The paper establishes no delayed jump, so whether the progress measure anticipates it cannot be shown. The authors say only that norm growth and accuracy improvement are simultaneous. 'Partial' overstates what this shows.

relationships.condition: GELU 2-layer MLP on mod-113 addition with 10% label noise and weight decay
relationships.reason: Fourier-sparse neurons grow while most neuron norms decay to 0 (R6). Their drive comes from clean data (R8). Frequency matching and phase alignment emerge progressively over epochs 500–2000 (R9).
relationships.display_finding: Clean data drives Fourier-sparse neuron growth while most neuron norms decay to zero, with frequency matching and phase alignment emerging progressively over epochs 500–2,000.

relationships.condition: GELU MLP with Adam and weight decay λ between 1e-4 and 5e-4
relationships.reason: With λ=0 there is no test generalization (R1). Moderate λ generalizes, and λ=5e-4 drops the noisy labels (R2, R3). Weight decay prunes all but the high-sparsity neurons (R6).
relationships.display_finding: Zero weight decay produced no test generalization, moderate decay enabled it, λ=0.0005 discarded noisy labels, and weight decay pruned all but the high-sparsity neurons.

relationships.reason: Too much weight decay prevents convergence entirely (R4). The low-norm bias works only within a window.
relationships.display_finding: The stronger weight-decay penalty prevented convergence entirely.
